summary.text: Arenes are typically split into two categories: benzoids, which contain a benzene derivative, and non-benzoids, which contain other aromatic cyclic derivatives.
Aromatic compounds are pervasive in nature and industry, and they are commonly used in organic synthesis.
Benzene is the least complex aromatic hydrocarbon, and benzene, toluene and xylene are the key industrial aromatic hydrocarbons.

facts.label: Industrial trio
facts.value: Benzene, toluene and xylene, called BTX

facts.label: Benzene bond order
facts.value: All six carbon–carbon bonds have order 1.5

facts.label: Circle symbol
facts.value: Introduced by Robinson and Armit in 1925

items.prompt: A chemist has an aromatic ring compound that contains no benzene derivative, only some other aromatic cyclic derivative. Where does it fall among arenes?

options.label: Among the non-benzoids, which hold other aromatic derivatives
Among the benzoids, which follow the benzene ring model
Nowhere, since arenes must all contain a benzene derivative
Among the heteroarenes, which must always contain sulfur

items.explain: Arenes split into benzoids, which contain a benzene derivative, and non-benzoids, which contain other aromatic cyclic derivatives.

items.prompt: A drawing of benzene shows alternating single and double bonds. How do the six carbon–carbon bonds really compare?

options.label: Three are long single bonds and three are short double bonds
All six are equivalent, with electrons shared around the ring
Two are double bonds and the other four are single bonds
All six are full double bonds with two electron pairs each

items.explain: The six ring electrons are shared equally in delocalized pi orbitals, giving six equivalent bonds of order 1.5.

items.prompt: Pyridine has a six-membered ring in which a nitrogen atom takes the place of one carbon. Can a ring like that still be aromatic?

options.label: No, since an aromatic ring may contain only carbon atoms
No, since nitrogen cannot take part in a ring of six atoms
Yes, since heteroarenes swap in oxygen, nitrogen or sulfur and stay aromatic
Yes, but only when it is combined with a second benzene ring

items.explain: Heteroarenes are aromatic compounds with a heteroatom in the ring, and pyridine is a named example.

items.prompt: A campfire burns wood. Could the fire produce polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons?

options.label: No, they form only when fossil fuels are burned
No, they exist only inside oil, coal and tar deposits
Yes, but only when the wood is burned in a closed vessel
Yes, they form as byproducts of burning fuel, including biomass

items.explain: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons occur in oil, coal and tar, and are made as byproducts of burning fossil fuel or biomass.

items.prompt: Phenol's OH group readily gives up its hydrogen as H+. What feature of the benzene ring helps this?

options.label: The ring pulls the extra hydrogen into the middle of the ring
The ring partly spreads the negative charge left on the oxygen
The ring makes the oxygen atom larger than a normal oxygen
The ring blocks the charge from ever touching the oxygen

items.explain: Arene rings can stabilize charges: in phenol the charge on the oxygen is partially delocalized into the ring.

items.prompt: A group on a benzene ring pulls electrons away from it. Where do new groups mostly get added?

options.label: At the ortho position
At the para position
On the same carbon as the existing group
At the meta position

items.explain: Deactivators, which are electron withdrawing, are meta directors, while electron-donating activators direct to ortho and para.

paragraphs.heading: Benzene and its family
paragraphs.text: Benzene, C₆H₆, is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon and the first compound to be defined as one. Aromatic compounds turn up all over nature and industry. Benzene, toluene and xylene, known together as BTX, are the key industrial ones. Many molecules in living things carry phenyl groups, among them the aromatic amino acids.

paragraphs.heading: How the benzene ring holds together
paragraphs.text: Joseph Loschmidt and August Kekulé each worked out benzene's bonding in the 19th century. Its carbons form a hexagon, and each carbon has four electrons to share. One goes into a sigma bond with a hydrogen, and one bonds to each of the two neighbouring carbons. The six electrons left over are shared evenly around the whole ring in delocalized pi orbitals as big as the ring itself. That is why all six carbon–carbon bonds are alike, each with a bond order of 1.5.

paragraphs.heading: Electrons above and below
paragraphs.text: The shared electrons are pictured as floating above and below the ring. The fields they create help keep the ring flat. The same equal bonds can also be explained with resonance forms.

paragraphs.heading: The circle symbol
paragraphs.text: Chemists often mark aromaticity with a circle symbol. Robert Robinson and his student James Armit introduced it in 1925, and the Morrison & Boyd organic chemistry textbook made it popular from 1959. How to use it is still argued over: some apply it to any cyclic π system, others only to those that obey Hückel's rule, and some would keep it for single rings with 6 π electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Groups on the ring
paragraphs.text: Benzene derivatives carry from one to six substituents on the ring. Phenol has one hydroxyl group and toluene one methyl group. With two or more, their positions matter, and they are labelled ortho, meta and para. Electron-donating substituents are called activators and steer new groups to the ortho and para positions, while electron-withdrawing deactivators steer them to meta.

paragraphs.heading: Counting the isomers of cresol
paragraphs.text: Cresol shows how this works. Its methyl and hydroxyl groups can sit side by side (ortho), one position apart (meta) or two positions apart (para), so three isomers exist. Both groups are ortho-para directors, so the ortho and para forms are usually favoured. Xylenol adds a second methyl group, and it has 6 isomers.

paragraphs.heading: Aromatic rings beyond benzene
paragraphs.text: Any ring that obeys Hückel's rule without being a benzene derivative can also count as aromatic. One example is the cyclopropenium cation, which meets the rule with n equal to 0. Other rings swap a carbon for a heteroatom such as nitrogen, oxygen or sulfur. Pyridine has a six-membered ring with one nitrogen, pyrrole a five-membered ring with nitrogen, and furan a five-membered ring with one oxygen.

paragraphs.heading: Fused rings
paragraphs.text: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs, are made of fused aromatic rings with no heteroatoms or substituents, and naphthalene is the simplest. They occur in oil, coal and tar, and they form when fossil fuels or biomass burn. Some have been found to be carcinogenic, mutagenic or teratogenic, so they are a concern as pollutants. Meat grilled or barbecued at high heat and smoked fish can hold high levels. In graphene the same fused-ring pattern stretches into large 2D sheets.
